newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish pension system needs overhaul.
newsitem.headline: Spanish pension system needs overhaul.

text.p: Spain, on the verge of finishing a public pension reform, must take even more radical measures to avoid a rise in public deficits and these steps should boost the private pension fund business.

"A deep reform is needed. Here in Spain a demographic problem is worsened by the high unemployment rate...More changes should be in the pipeline," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
An ageing population is expected to absorb a growing part of public spending in the next century.

Unemployment is running at above 20 percent, twice the European Union average. Still, a late baby boom has left Spain with younger citizens and more time to overhaul the system than France or Germany.

"According to different studies, the current system can survive until 2000 or 2010, but then it will need drastic reform. It's just a matter of time. Our welfare payments are among the best in Europe," said Angel Martinez-Aldama, chief economist at Inverco, association of Spain's pension funds.

Spain is expected to pour 3.63 trillion pesetas into social security this year, up 5.4 percent from last year, according to the 1997 budget. These figures also take into account some health system expenditure.

If no changes are introduced the current balanced account could fall to deficit of 1.4 percent of gross domestic product in 2000 and to six percent in 2050, according to a recent study by Spain's Catalonian Bank la Caixa.

In 2050, inflows from workers will cover only 55.6 percent of expenditure. At that point, either pension payments must be cut by more than 45 pct or contributions must be increased by more than 80 pct, the study said.
State spending on pensions in 1996 is estimated at 7.5 trillion pesetas.
Private pension funds were introduced in 1987, but have grown only slowly and assets reached 2.5 trillion pesetas last September.
The government's deal with unions in October 1996, which is still not yet law, introduced small changes to the system to guarantee its viability until 2000.
The deal hopes to adjust pension payments annually to current inflation and will increase the minimum number of years of contribution.
In a recent study, UGT, one of Spain's biggest unions, said that past reforms had increased the portion the central government pays to the public pension system.
That share rose from 9.48 percent of the total social security's funds in 1980 to 27.98 percent in 1995.
Economists attributed private pension funds' slow take-off to the already substantial contributions workers are making to the public system. But growth has accelerated recently.
"What we are currently doing is to ask younger workers to pay for something they won't receive at the end," Urrutia said.

In September 1996, the last month for which data are available, total pension fund assets were up 36 percent over the year-earlier month. Assets were expected to have risen to three trillion pesetas by year end from September's 2.5 trillion, Inverco said.
While waiting for a more thorough reform, Inverco asked the government to make certain changes to boost inflows into pension funds.

"We asked the government to make these funds redeemable after a certain amount of years, to reduce taxes and to increase the maximum amount of money people can invest each year, which now stands at a one million pesetas," said Martinez-Aldama.
But other measures could also help.
"It would be interesting to allow people the possibility to pay into the same pension fund while moving from one company to another," added Urrutia.
